We had forty five minutes of light. We used the last five.

This is the part nobody puts in the reel. A road through the polder, a bag of batteries in the van, and a lot of looking at the sky to see what the clouds are doing.

The shot list said golden hour. The weather said clouded over. So we waited.

People think aerial work is about the drone. It is not. It is about timing. You get one window where the light is low and warm and the grass goes gold. Everything before that is preparation so you do not waste a second of it.

Then there was the van. The little blue bus that drives out of the village had to hit the bend at the exact moment the drone came over the treeline. Too early and it is gone before the frame opens. Too late and you are looking at an empty road. It took a few runs and a radio to get it right. In post we graded it purple, so it reads as one accent in all that green instead of just a car.

The Inspire 3 gives us full frame, clean noise and a cinematic image with high dynamic range. Useful, but it is still just a camera on a stick that flies. The choice of where to put it is the actual work.

So yes, this is the glamour. One person, one field, one drone, and a sky that is deciding whether to cooperate.

It did, right at the end. Around eight the clouds broke for about five minutes and the whole polder went warm. We got the shot on the very last battery.

If you are planning something that needs air, tell us early. We can build the ground schedule around the light instead of hoping for it.
